items.title: US Midterm Election Results 2026 impact: What Trump's loss mean for Sensex, Nifty, gold, silver rates? Experts' views
points: US Midterm Election Results 2026: The Democrats have secured control of both chambers of the US Congress in the 2026 midterm elections, marking a significant setback for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

items.title: Propspeed Joins RightShip’s Zero Harm Innovation Partners Program to Support More Efficient and Sustainable Vessel Operations
points: Improving vessel energy efficiency is an important part of the maritime industry’s efforts to reduce fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions.

Through the Program, Propspeed aims to raise awareness of the role propeller surface condition plays in vessel performance and how coating technologies can help shipowners and managers manage efficiency losses associated with biofouling and propeller…

items.title: NAPA on why wind-assisted ships need proof of savings, not just a contract
points: A contract for sharing savings, however, only works if both parties can agree on what the savings were.
That is where wind-assisted shipping still has a gap.

According to the International Windship Association, more than 100 commercial ships now sail with wind propulsion fitted, totalling over six million deadweight tonnes, and around 100 more are on order.
Retrofits are typically saving between 5% – 20% of fuel in service, with the variation dependent on trade route, prevailing winds and the size of the sails relative to the ship’s installed power.

A credible approach maps wind along the whole route before departure, reassesses it against swell, wind waves and current, and states savings in dollars rather than percentages, so operators can see the financial case for a routing decision before…
NAPA’s performance models start from the ship’s 3D hull form and hydrodynamics and are calibrated with operational data.

items.title: Seafarer experience must shape maritime technology, initial STEER Project report finds
points: Technology can improve safety, efficiency and life at sea, but its benefits depend heavily on how systems are designed, introduced, supported and used, according to initial findings from the STEER Project.

The Nautical Institute, in collaboration with Lloyd’s Register Foundation, has published The evidence, the gaps and the way forward, its initial report into understanding how technology impacts seafarers.
A review of 471 maritime casualty cases between 2005 and 2025 found that 43.1% involved at least one human-factor cause associated with equipment and workplace conditions.
Among 35 cases where technology was identified as the direct cause, safety management failures were present in 89% and inadequate resourcing in 77%.

David Patraiko, Director of Projects, The Nautical Institute said: “Technology is bringing significant benefits to shipping, but the evidence shows that those benefits cannot be judged on technical capability alone.
The research draws on 105 academic studies, 55 industry publications and 471 casualty reports, alongside direct engagement with seafarers and other maritime professionals.

items.title: NGOs Welcome Greenland Scrubber Ban, Urges IMO, other Arctic Countries to Follow Lead
points: Greenland will ban open loop scrubbers from July 1st, 2027, and closed loop scrubbers from July 1st, 2029 in inland waterways and territorial seas.

The adopted proposal says that ”Naalakkersuisut is directed to introduce a ban, effective from 1 July 2027, on discharges from open-loop exhaust gas cleaning systems within Greenland’s port areas, internal waters, and territorial waters.

From 1 July 2029, the ban on the discharge of exhaust gas cleaning water will apply to all systems.” Greenland’s ban on scrubbers — also known as Exhaust Gas Cleaning Systems (EGCS) — follows a Danish ban which came into effect on July 1st, 2025.

Greenland’s ban aligns with that of Denmark, which also banned scrubber discharges, along with other ambitious Nordic countries like Sweden and Finland that have similar bans in territorial seas, and with an OSPAR recommendation agreed in 2025.

items.title: Supreme Court calls for fresh look at 2-child norms
points: Emphasising that India must guard against a potentially irreversible decline in fertility and frame policies in tune with changing demographic realities, a bench of justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe referred the matter to a larger bench for…
The court observed that the assumptions underlying the earlier ruling in Javed Vs State of Haryana had been overtaken by demographic changes and could no longer be treated as valid.

According to a compilation placed before the court by amicus curiae Rukmini Bobde, the restriction is currently in force at least in six states — Assam, Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha and Uttarakhand.

items.title: Armed forces need a balance of youth, experience: Chief of Defence Staff
points: “It will enhance the youthful profile of the armed forces and provide them a fresh lease of ‘josh’ (enthusiasm) and ‘jazba’ (passion).
It is envisaged that average age profile of Indian armed forces would come down by 4-5 years by implementation of this scheme,” the defence ministry said at the time.
The shift from releasing 75% of Agniveers after four years to retaining all of them for full-term service marks a sharp departure from the original plan.
Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani on Wednesday said that one of the principal reasons for the rethink was that the character of warfare has changed in the last few years.

The changes meet the requirement of the armed forces, both in terms of having a youthful, motivated force, as well as having a mature and technology-enabled force,” he said at a joint cabinet briefing on Wednesday with Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw.
